# `Reactily.createContextProvider`

Creates a provider element for a Reactily context.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createContextProvider<T>(contextValue: Context<T>, value: T, children: {any}, key: string?): Element
```
## Usage
```luau
local provider = Reactily.createContextProvider(
	Context,
	value,
	{
		child,
	}
)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createContext`, `useContext`, component trees.

## Understanding this API

Advanced component utilities change how Reactily constructs, loads, wraps, or reuses part of the virtual tree. Their behavior affects rendering and component boundaries, not the underlying Roblox Instance class directly.

### Practical guidance

Choose these only when you need their particular behavior; ordinary user interfaces can be built with typed creators and `createComponent`. Understand the component lifecycle and return type before adding wrappers.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this creator when you need the ContextProvider capability described above, and keep its result under a clear owner.

### Behavior and ownership

Component helpers affect how an element is wrapped, loaded, or constructed inside the virtual tree.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** A component wrapper does not become a Roblox Instance until rendered by a root.

# `Reactily.createContext`

Creates a typed Reactily context with a fallback value.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createContext<T>(defaultValue: T): Context<T>
```
## Usage
```luau
local Context = Reactily.createContext({
	Enabled = true,
})
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createContextProvider`, `useContext`, `memo`.

## Understanding this API

Advanced component utilities change how Reactily constructs, loads, wraps, or reuses part of the virtual tree. Their behavior affects rendering and component boundaries, not the underlying Roblox Instance class directly.

### Practical guidance

Choose these only when you need their particular behavior; ordinary user interfaces can be built with typed creators and `createComponent`. Understand the component lifecycle and return type before adding wrappers.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use context when a subtree needs the same configuration or state without threading the value through every intermediate component.

### Behavior and ownership

`createContext` defines the context identity and a fallback value; a provider supplies a value to consumers.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Define contexts once at module scope, not on every component render.

# `Reactily.createErrorBoundary`

Creates an error boundary around one child element.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createErrorBoundary(fallback: Element | ((failure: any) -> Element), child: Element, onError: ((failure: any) -> ())?, key: string?): Element
```
## Usage
```luau
local boundary = Reactily.createErrorBoundary(
	errorFallback,
	child,
	function(failure)
		warn(failure)
	end
)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createSuspense`, `lazy`, `createResource`.

## Understanding this API

An error boundary provides fallback UI when descendant rendering fails.

### Practical guidance

It does not generally replace every Lua `pcall` around ordinary event handlers. Use a meaningful fallback and log the underlying error while developing.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use an error boundary to show fallback UI when descendant rendering fails.

### Behavior and ownership

The boundary catches supported render-time failures in its subtree.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Do not assume it catches every Roblox event callback or asynchronous task error.

# `Reactily.createResource`

Creates a lazy resource whose loader runs only when first requested.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createResource<T>(loader: () -> T): Resource<T>
```
## Usage
```luau
local Resource = Reactily.createResource(function()
	return loadData()
end)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createSuspense`, `createErrorBoundary`, lazy asynchronous UI.

## Understanding this API

Advanced component utilities change how Reactily constructs, loads, wraps, or reuses part of the virtual tree. Their behavior affects rendering and component boundaries, not the underlying Roblox Instance class directly.

### Practical guidance

Choose these only when you need their particular behavior; ordinary user interfaces can be built with typed creators and `createComponent`. Understand the component lifecycle and return type before adding wrappers.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this for lazily obtained data that is accessed from the component/resource flow, rather than creating ad-hoc loader calls in render.

### Behavior and ownership

The resource holds its loader and exposes the resource contract. Its behavior integrates with supported Suspense flows.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Handle failures with the supported error-boundary flow. A resource is not a Roblox Instance and should not be parented.

# `Reactily.createSuspense`

Creates a Suspense boundary around one child element.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createSuspense(fallback: Element, child: Element, key: string?): Element
```
## Usage
```luau
local boundary = Reactily.createSuspense(
	loadingFallback,
	child
)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createResource`, `lazy`, `createErrorBoundary`.

## Understanding this API

Suspense provides fallback UI while a child waits for a compatible pending resource or lazy operation.

### Practical guidance

Design the fallback for short or repeated waits. Resource handling must follow Reactily’s supported suspense behavior; ordinary `task.wait()` in arbitrary components is not equivalent.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use Suspense to display fallback elements while supported lazy/resource work is unresolved.

### Behavior and ownership

The boundary coordinates an alternative element until its children are ready.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Make fallback content simple and avoid triggering resource reads from that fallback.

# `Reactily.forwardRef`

Creates a component wrapper that forwards props.ref to the render callback.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.forwardRef(render: (props: any, Ref: RefTarget<any>?) -> any): any
```
## Usage
```luau
local input = Reactily.forwardRef(function(props, Ref)
	return Reactily.createTextBox({
		Ref = Ref,
		Text = props.text,
	})
end)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `useImperativeHandle`, `useRef`, typed host refs.

## Understanding this API

Ref forwarding allows a component wrapper to expose a child ref instead of preventing callers from reaching the target.

### Practical guidance

Use this for reusable wrappers around focusable controls or GUI elements when consumers genuinely need access to the inner host Instance.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use a forwarded ref when a reusable component must expose a host instance or imperative handle to its caller.

### Behavior and ownership

The ref is forwarded through the wrapper instead of being treated as an ordinary prop.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Keep ref ownership explicit and expect a cleared ref after the component unmounts.

# `Reactily.lazy`

Creates a component whose implementation is loaded on first render.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.lazy<T>(loader: () -> T): T
```
## Usage
```luau
local panel = Reactily.lazy(function()
	return require(script.Parent.Panel)
end)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `preloadLazy`, `createSuspense`, `createErrorBoundary`.

## Understanding this API

Lazy component loading postpones resolving a component until it is needed.

### Practical guidance

Use Suspense with an appropriate fallback for work that can be temporarily unavailable; do not rely on a lazy component being resolved synchronously.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use lazy components when construction or loading should be deferred until needed.

### Behavior and ownership

A lazy wrapper delays access to the component implementation until the supported loading path runs.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Provide appropriate fallback and error behavior for components that can be unavailable while loading.

# `Reactily.memo`

Wraps a component with a memoization comparator.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.memo<T>(componentValue: T, comparator: ((previousProps: {[string]: any}, nextProps: {[string]: any}) -> boolean)?): T
```
## Usage
```luau
local optimizedComponent = Reactily.memo(Component)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `shallowEqual`, selectors, immutable `patch`, context.

## Understanding this API

Memo wraps a component to skip work when the comparison reports that relevant props have not changed.

### Practical guidance

Use this for expensive children that frequently receive the same props. Incorrect comparators can hide necessary updates, so start with the default behavior and profile before optimizing.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this wrapper to avoid unnecessary recomputation of components when their inputs have not meaningfully changed.

### Behavior and ownership

The wrapper can skip work when its equality decision says inputs are unchanged.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Do not rely on memoization to hide side effects inside a render function.

# `Reactily.createAnimationDelay`

Creates a one-shot delay step compatible with Reactily animation sequences.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createAnimationDelay(seconds: number): AnimationPlayable
```
## Usage
```luau
local delay = Reactily.createAnimationDelay(.2)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createTween`, `parallelAnimations`, `sequenceAnimations`, `useOwned`.

## Understanding this API

This animation operation fits into Reactily’s handling of time-based UI behavior. Check the return type carefully: composing a sequence, creating a spring, and playing a Tween have different lifetime and playback rules.

### Practical guidance

Review the return type before using the result: an animation handle may need to be played and eventually cleaned up, whereas a transition helper may schedule an existing callback. Keep native property names in official Roblox casing.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this creator when you need the AnimationDelay capability described above, and keep its result under a clear owner.

### Behavior and ownership

Animation helpers have different ownership and playback behavior. Review the return type before composing them.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Do not assume every animation helper returns a Tween or starts playing immediately.

# `Reactily.createSpring`

Creates a spring for number, Vector2, Vector3, or Color3 values.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createSpring<T>(initialValue: T, options: SpringOptions?): Spring<T>
```
## Usage
```luau
local Spring = Reactily.createSpring(0, {
	frequency = 8,
	damping = 1,
})

Spring.setTarget(1)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `useSpring`, bindings, component-owned lifecycle.

## Understanding this API

This animation operation fits into Reactily’s handling of time-based UI behavior. Check the return type carefully: composing a sequence, creating a spring, and playing a Tween have different lifetime and playback rules.

### Practical guidance

Review the return type before using the result: an animation handle may need to be played and eventually cleaned up, whereas a transition helper may schedule an existing callback. Keep native property names in official Roblox casing.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use a spring when a changing value needs smooth, spring-like motion.

### Behavior and ownership

Its target and current value follow the spring’s configured behavior; the result is not itself a TweenService Tween.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Check the expected spring option keys and supported value types before configuring it.

# `Reactily.createTween`

Creates an owned TweenService animation without playing it immediately.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createTween(
	instance: Instance,
	goals: {[string]: any},
	options: TweenOptions
): Animation
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `instance` | `Instance` | Yes | Roblox Instance used by the requested Reactily helper. |
| `goals` | `{[string]: any}` | Yes | Roblox TweenService goal property table. |
| `options` | `TweenOptions` | Yes | Typed Tween configuration. |

## Returns

An owned `Animation` handle with PascalCase `Play()`, `Cancel()`, `Delete()`, and `IsDeleted()` methods.

## Usage
```luau
local Animation = Reactily.createTween(Frame, {
	BackgroundTransparency = 0,
}, {
	Time = 0.2,
})
Animation.Play()
```

## Understanding this API

This creates a managed TweenService animation targeting an existing Instance. The returned animation is separate from the virtual element tree.

### Practical guidance

Creation alone does not play it. Keep the handle to start, cancel, and delete the animation as its owning UI component or controller is cleaned up.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this creator when you need the Tween capability described above, and keep its result under a clear owner.

### Behavior and ownership

Animation helpers have different ownership and playback behavior. Review the return type before composing them.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Do not assume every animation helper returns a Tween or starts playing immediately.

# `Reactily.createViewTransition`

Creates a ViewTransition element with optional transition callbacks and configuration. This export is included in Reactily v2.2.0 (API v1).

## Signature

```luau
Reactily.createViewTransition(child: Element, config: {[string]: any}?, onEnter: ((...any) -> ())?, onExit: ((...any) -> ())?, onUpdate: ((...any) -> ())?, key: string?): Element
```

## Usage

```luau
local transition = Reactily.createViewTransition(panel, { Duration = 0.2 })
```

Use this hook or constructor only in a valid Reactily component/render context, as applicable.

## Understanding this API

ViewTransition coordinates callbacks and visual state changes between different mounted views.

### Practical guidance

Provide reliable enter/update/exit behavior and clean up any work initiated by the transition when the related UI is removed.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use view transitions when changing between UI states and coordinating their enter/update/exit phases.

### Behavior and ownership

The specialized component coordinates callbacks around a change in rendered view.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Keep transitions safe if the component unmounts while a transition is pending.

### Behavior and ownership

# `Reactily.bindAttribute`

Binds a reactive value to a Roblox Attribute with optional two-way synchronization.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.bindAttribute<T>(source: Binding<T>, instance: Instance, attributeName: string, twoWay: boolean?): () -> ()
```
## Usage
```luau
local cleanup = Reactily.bindAttribute(
	enabledBinding,
	instance,
	"Enabled",
	true
)

cleanup()
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createBinding`, `mapBinding`, `combineBindings`, `combineBindingsMany`.

## Understanding this API

This connects a binding with a Roblox Attribute stored on an Instance. Attributes can be read or observed by other scripts.

### Practical guidance

Use a real Attribute name, not a property name. The optional two-way setting changes whether external attribute updates can flow back into the binding.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use when an Instance attribute should track a binding value.

### Behavior and ownership

The binding writes the named Roblox attribute as values change.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Attribute values must be valid Roblox attribute types; unsupported values cannot be stored on Instances.

# `Reactily.bindProperty`

Binds a reactive value to a Roblox property with optional two-way synchronization.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.bindProperty<T>(source: Binding<T>, instance: Instance, propertyName: string, twoWay: boolean?): () -> ()
```
## Usage
```luau
local cleanup = Reactily.bindProperty(
	positionBinding,
	frame,
	"Position",
	true
)

cleanup()
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createBinding`, `mapBinding`, `combineBindings`, `combineBindingsMany`.

## Understanding this API

This connects a binding to a named property of an existing Roblox Instance. Changes propagate to that property without constructing a new virtual element.

### Practical guidance

The property name is a Roblox property string, such as `"BackgroundTransparency"`; use official casing and clean up the binding when the target is no longer needed.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use when an existing Roblox Instance property should follow a binding value.

### Behavior and ownership

The binding manages future property updates after it is attached.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** The target must support the named property. Preserve exact native Roblox property casing.

# `Reactily.clampBinding`

Creates a derived numeric binding clamped between `minimum` and `maximum`.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.clampBinding(
	source: Binding<number>,
	minimum: number,
	maximum: number
): Binding<number>
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `source` | `Binding<number>` | Yes | Source Reactily atom, binding, or signal. |
| `minimum` | `number` | Yes | Minimum allowed numeric value. |
| `maximum` | `number` | Yes | Maximum allowed value or maximum number of signal emissions to forward. |

## Returns

A `Binding<number>`.

## Usage
```luau
local safeProgress = Reactily.clampBinding(progress, 0, 1)
```

## Understanding this API

Bindings connect a changing value to dependent values or Roblox properties. They are useful when values update repeatedly and you want to avoid rebuilding unrelated parts of a component tree.

### Practical guidance

When a binding is attached to a Roblox Instance or subscribed to another source, keep and invoke any returned cleanup function when its owner is destroyed. Use a mapped binding to transform values and a direct property binding when the target is a native Roblox property.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this helper when creates a derived numeric binding clamped between minimum and maximum.

### Behavior and ownership

A binding represents changing data that can be observed or transformed.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Avoid keeping subscriptions alive after the target Instance or owning UI is removed.

# `Reactily.combineBindingsMany`

## Signature

```luau
Reactily.useAttribute<T>(
	instance: Instance,
	attributeName: string,
	defaultValue: T
): (T, (value: T) -> ())
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `instance` | `Instance` | Yes | Roblox Instance used by the requested Reactily helper. |
| `attributeName` | `string` | Yes | Roblox Attribute name owned or observed by this Reactily state helper. |
| `defaultValue` | `T` | Yes | Fallback value used when the Roblox Attribute currently has no value. |

## Returns

An Attribute is not a native property; use the attribute key passed to `GetAttribute` or `SetAttribute` rather than a Roblox property name.

# `Reactily.useCallback`

Memoizes a callback/value by dependency array.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.useCallback<T>(callback: T, dependencies: {any}?): T
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `callback` | `T` | Yes | Function Reactily calls for the operation, subscription, effect, batch, scheduled task, or event. |
| `dependencies` | `{any}?` | No | Dependency array used to decide whether the memo, callback, or effect should update. `nil` means it is treated as changed every render. |

## Returns

`T`.

## Usage
```luau
local OnClick = Reactily.useCallback(function()
	print(selection)
end, {selection})
```

## Understanding this API

Use this when a callback should retain its identity between renders, for example when passing it into a memoized child component.

### Practical guidance

`useCallback` does not itself prevent every rerender. It only stabilizes the callback reference while dependencies remain unchanged.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this hook when the component needs memoizes a callback/value by dependency array.

### Behavior and ownership

This hook participates in component lifecycle and must be invoked in consistent order during rendering.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Calling this hook conditionally or from ordinary utility code can break hook ordering. Use it only in supported render contexts.


```luau
local Value = Reactily.useContext(Context)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `createContext`, `createContextProvider`, `memo`.

## Understanding this API

Context makes a shared value available to descendants without manually passing it through every intermediate component.

### Practical guidance

A matching provider must exist above the consumer when the application requires a provided value; use context for shared dependencies, not for high-frequency per-object updates.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use `useContext` to read a value supplied by the nearest matching context provider.

### Behavior and ownership

The read is associated with a component’s render; the context must be the one created by `createContext`.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Creating a new context object during each render prevents consumers from sharing the intended provider.

# `Reactily.useEffect`

Runs an effect after a completed component render and supports cleanup.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.useEffect(callback: () -> (() -> ())?, dependencies: {any}?)
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `callback` | `() -> (() -> ())?` | Yes | Runs after the component renders; may return a cleanup callback. |
| `dependencies` | `{any}?` | No | Re-runs the effect when a dependency changes. |

## Returns

No value.

## Usage
```luau
Reactily.useEffect(function()
	local Connection = Signal:Connect(onChanged)

	return function()
		Connection:Disconnect()
	end
end, {Signal})
```

## Understanding this API

An effect is for work performed outside rendering, such as connecting a Roblox event, subscribing to a signal, or coordinating an external Instance.

### Practical guidance

Return a cleanup function to disconnect or undo previous work. The dependencies array controls when the effect must be reconsidered; omitting or changing dependencies affects how often it runs.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use an effect to synchronize a mounted component with subscriptions, time-based work, or external Roblox objects.

### Behavior and ownership

The effect runs as part of Reactily’s managed lifecycle. Return a cleanup callback when creating a subscription or connection.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Avoid starting a new event connection on every render without disconnecting the previous one.

# `Reactily.useMemo`

Memoizes a calculated value by dependency array.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.useMemo<T>(factory: () -> T, dependencies: {any}?): T
```

| `factory` | `() -> T, dependencies: {any}?` | No | Function that calculates and returns the memoized value. |

## Returns

`T`.


Include every changing input that the calculation reads in the dependency list. A stale dependency list can produce stale results; use a normal local computation for inexpensive work.

## Additional usage notes

A memoized value is an optimization, not a separate source of truth.

`useState` gives a function component a state value and a stable setter. When that value changes, Reactily schedules the component for an update.

## When to use it

Use `useState` for values that belong to one component, such as a counter, selected tab, or whether a menu is open. For shared state outside the component tree, consider an [atom](/docs/api/state/create-atom) or a store instead.

## Signature

```luau
Reactily.useState<T>(initialValue: T): (T, StateSetter<T>)
```

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `initialValue` | `T` | Value used when the component first mounts. |

## Returns

Two values: the current state and a setter that accepts a value or an updater function.

## Example: interactive counter

```luau
local function Counter(): Reactily.Element
    local count, setCount = Reactily.useState(0)

    return Reactily.createTextButton({
        Size = UDim2.fromOffset(220, 48),
        Text = `Count: {count}`,
        OnActivated = function()
            setCount(function(previous: number): number
                return previous + 1
            end)
        end,
    })
end
```

Render it with `Reactily.createComponent(Counter, {})` inside a root.

## Important notes

- Call hooks at the top level of a component, in the same order on every render.
- Use the functional setter when the next value depends on the previous state.
- Setting a state value does not directly mutate Roblox Instances; Reactily handles reconciliation.

## Related

[Getting Started](/docs/getting-started) · [State and Reactivity](/docs/concepts/state) · [Examples](/docs/guides/examples)

## Understanding this API

Use this for information a component must remember between renders, such as a selected tab or an input value. The setter schedules another render rather than immediately changing a Roblox Instance.

### Practical guidance

When the next value depends on the previous one, pass an updater function to the setter; this avoids depending on a stale value captured by an earlier callback.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use component-local state for interaction values that should trigger a rerender, such as a selected tab or open menu.

### Behavior and ownership

Reactily retains the state value across ordinary renders and schedules an update after its setter is called.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Do not change the number or order of hooks between renders. For updates based on the old value, use a functional setter.

# `Reactily.Children`

`Reactily.Children` is a public namespace exported by the runtime. Its methods are listed below.

## Understanding this namespace

Use this namespace when a component accepts arbitrary child values or nested child arrays and needs to normalize them consistently. `toArray` produces a flat list, `count` reports its length, and `only` asserts that exactly one normalized child was supplied.

Use the lowercase/camelCase methods shown in the signatures below. Roblox engine properties such as `Size`, `Position`, `BackgroundColor3`, and `ViewportSize` retain their official PascalCase names.

## Methods

### `Children.count`

Counts normalized Reactily children.

```luau
Reactily.Children.count(children: { any }): number
```

### `Children.forEach`

Invokes a callback for every normalized child.

```luau
Reactily.Children.forEach(children: { any }, callback: (child: Reactily.Element, index: number) -> ())
```

### `Children.map`

Maps normalized children and flattens returned child arrays.

```luau
Reactily.Children.map( children: { any }, callback: (child: Reactily.Element, index: number) -> any ): { Reactily.Element }
```

### `Children.only`

Returns the only normalized child and errors when the count differs from one.

```luau
Reactily.Children.only(children: { any }): Reactily.Element
```

### `Children.toArray`

Flattens nested children into a new ordered array.

```luau
Reactily.Children.toArray(children: { any }): { Reactily.Element }
```

## Example: normalize optional children

```luau
local first = Reactily.createTextLabel({ Text = "First" })
local second = Reactily.createTextLabel({ Text = "Second" })
local input = { first, { second } }

local flattened = Reactily.Children.toArray(input)
print(Reactily.Children.count(input)) -- 2
print(Reactily.Children.only({ first }) == first) -- true
```

**Choosing a method:** Use `count` to inspect the number of normalized children; `forEach` for side-effect-free inspection; `map` when creating a transformed child list; `only` when an API accepts exactly one child; and `toArray` when passing a flattened array into a different helper. `only` raises an error when zero or multiple children remain after normalization.

## Notes and common mistakes

- **Input:** Nested child lists are normalized before applying `count`, `forEach`, `map`, `only`, or `toArray`.
- **Common mistake:** Calling `only` with zero or more than one normalized child raises an error. Use `toArray` when the number is not fixed.

# `Reactily.Layout`

`Reactily.Layout` is a public namespace exported by the runtime. Its methods are listed below.

## Understanding this namespace

Use the layout helpers to construct transparent containers plus the relevant Roblox layout objects. The choice between `horizontal`, `vertical`, `wrap`, and `grid` changes how children are arranged; the result is still a virtual Reactily element.

Use the lowercase/camelCase methods shown in the signatures below. Roblox engine properties such as `Size`, `Position`, `BackgroundColor3`, and `ViewportSize` retain their official PascalCase names.

## Methods

### `Layout.horizontal`

Creates a transparent horizontal list container.

```luau
Reactily.Layout.horizontal(options: ListOptions?, children: { any }): Reactily.Element
```

### `Layout.vertical`

Creates a transparent vertical list container.

```luau
Reactily.Layout.vertical(options: ListOptions?, children: { any }): Reactily.Element
```

### `Layout.wrap`

Creates a transparent wrapping list container.

```luau
Reactily.Layout.wrap(options: ListOptions?, children: { any }): Reactily.Element
```

### `Layout.grid`

Creates a grid container backed by UIGridLayout.

```luau
Reactily.Layout.grid(options: GridOptions, children: { any }): Reactily.Element
```

### `Layout.stack`

Creates a transparent stacking container where children share the same bounds.

```luau
Reactily.Layout.stack(options: CommonOptions?, children: { any }): Reactily.Element
```

### `Layout.center`

Creates a container whose children are centered by UIListLayout.

```luau
Reactily.Layout.center(options: CommonOptions?, children: { any }): Reactily.Element
```

## Example: group elements horizontally

```luau
local layout = Reactily.Layout.horizontal(nil, {
    Reactily.createTextLabel({ Text = "Left" }),
    Reactily.createTextLabel({ Text = "Right" }),
})

local root = Reactily.createRoot(playerGui)
root.render(layout)
```

**Choosing a method:** `horizontal` and `vertical` use linear list arrangements; `wrap` handles multi-row content; `grid` is appropriate for fixed-size cells. Use `stack` when children should share a container, or `center` when the content must be centered. These helpers return virtual elements and do not mount UI until a root renders them.

## Notes and common mistakes

- **Input:** Layout helpers build virtual GUI compositions, not immediate Roblox layout Instances.
- **Common mistake:** Confusing native Roblox layout properties (`FillDirection`, `HorizontalAlignment`, etc.) with Reactily helper names.

# `Reactily.Profiler`

`Reactily.Profiler` is a public namespace exported by the runtime. Its methods are listed below.

## Understanding this namespace

The `Profiler` namespace contains measurement controls as well as a callable profiler component. Enable measurement before recording; use snapshots and slow-component lists to inspect observed rendering behavior.

Use the lowercase/camelCase methods shown in the signatures below. Roblox engine properties such as `Size`, `Position`, `BackgroundColor3`, and `ViewportSize` retain their official PascalCase names.

## Methods

### `Profiler.clear`

Clears all collected profiler data.

```luau
Reactily.Profiler.clear()
```

### `Profiler.isEnabled`

Returns whether component profiling is enabled.

```luau
Reactily.Profiler.isEnabled(): boolean
```

### `Profiler.get`

Returns a copy of profile data for one component.

```luau
Reactily.Profiler.get(componentValue: Component): ComponentProfile?
```

### `Profiler.snapshot`

Returns all currently collected component profiles.

```luau
Reactily.Profiler.snapshot(): profileMap
```

### `Profiler.getSlowComponents`

Returns the slowest recorded components ordered by average render time.

```luau
Reactily.Profiler.getSlowComponents(limit: number?): { slowComponent }
```

### `Profiler.record`

Records one component render when profiling is enabled.

```luau
Reactily.Profiler.record(componentValue: Component, duration: number, reason: string)
```

### `Profiler.setEnabled`

Enables or disables component profiling.

```luau
Reactily.Profiler.setEnabled(value: boolean)
```

## Reading profiler results

Enable recording first, reproduce the interaction you want to measure, and then inspect the results. `get` gives the profile for one component function; `snapshot` gives copies of the recorded profiles; `getSlowComponents` sorts the profiles by average render time. The `renderCount`, `averageTime`, and `totalTime` values should be interpreted together.

Calling `clear` empties the collected data without replacing the profiler module. This is useful before measuring a new interaction, so samples from an unrelated earlier test do not skew your investigation.

## Notes and common mistakes

- **Input:** Pass the same component function identity that is rendered, not the element returned from that function.
- **Common mistake:** Expecting an unprofiled component to have stats. Enable profiling before collecting samples.

# `Reactily.Props`

`Reactily.Props` is a public namespace exported by the runtime. Its methods are listed below.

## Understanding this namespace

These helpers work with plain props tables. `defaults` fills absent keys, `merge` combines tables, `pick` and `omit` filter keys, while `equal` and `changed` compare prop sets.

Use the lowercase/camelCase methods shown in the signatures below. Roblox engine properties such as `Size`, `Position`, `BackgroundColor3`, and `ViewportSize` retain their official PascalCase names.

## Methods

### `Props.defaults`

Returns a copy of props with missing values filled from defaults.

```luau
Reactily.Props.defaults<T>(props: T, defaults: PropMap): T
```

### `Props.equal`

Returns whether two prop tables are shallowly equal.

```luau
Reactily.Props.equal(first: PropMap, second: PropMap): boolean
```

### `Props.changed`

Returns changed current values plus keys that were removed.

```luau
Reactily.Props.changed(previous: PropMap, current: PropMap): (PropMap, { any })
```

### `Props.merge`

Merges prop tables from left to right without mutating any input.

```luau
Reactily.Props.merge(...: PropMap): PropMap
```

### `Props.omit`

Returns a copy without the supplied keys.

```luau
Reactily.Props.omit(props: PropMap, keys: { any }): PropMap
```

### `Props.pick`

Returns a new table containing only the supplied keys.

```luau
Reactily.Props.pick(props: PropMap, keys: { any }): PropMap
```

## Example: apply defaults and compare props

```luau
local props = Reactily.Props.defaults({ Text = "Ready" }, {
    Text = "Untitled",
    TextSize = 18,
})

local changed = Reactily.Props.changed({ Text = "Old" }, props)
print(props.Text, props.TextSize)
print(changed.Text)
```

**Choosing a method:** `defaults` only fills missing values, while `merge` lets later tables override earlier ones. `equal` performs a shallow comparison, and `changed` also reports removed keys in a second return value. `pick` and `omit` return new tables rather than modifying the original props table.

## Notes and common mistakes

- **Input:** Property utilities work on Reactily property tables; they do not modify a host Instance until those properties are rendered or explicitly applied.
- **Common mistake:** Expecting `pick`, `omit`, or `merge` to perform host mutation.

# Compatibility policy

Reactily follows semantic-versioning rules for its public API.

- Patch releases fix bugs without intentionally changing public contracts.
- Minor releases may add optional APIs and capabilities while preserving existing supported calls.
- Major releases may remove deprecated APIs or make intentionally breaking changes.

## Prefer capability checks

When adopting optional features, prefer checking whether the feature exists instead of requiring one exact patch version.

```luau
if Reactily.useOptimistic then
	-- use the newer capability
end
```

## Deprecation rule

Public APIs should be deprecated before removal. A replacement should ship first, old code should keep working through the current major line, and removal should wait for the next major release.

# `Reactily.createInstancePool`

Creates a bounded reusable pool for Roblox Instances of one class.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createInstancePool(className: string, maximumSize: number): ObjectPool<Instance>
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `className` | `string` | Yes | Roblox Instance class name to create or pool. |
| `maximumSize` | `number` | Yes | Maximum number of released objects retained by the pool. |

## Returns

A bounded `ObjectPool<Instance>`.

## Usage
```luau
local pool = Reactily.createInstancePool("Frame", 64)
local frame = pool.acquire()
pool.release(frame)
```

## Understanding this API

Instance pooling can reduce repeated Roblox Instance creation when you frequently show and hide similar objects.

### Practical guidance

Make sure a recycled Instance is reset before reuse, including properties and connections owned by its previous user.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this creator when you need the InstancePool capability described above, and keep its result under a clear owner.

### Behavior and ownership

Runtime helpers manage reusable objects, cleanup, and ownership details.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Make sure resources are returned to their owner or released when no longer needed.


# `Reactily.createAtom`

Creates standalone change-only typed state.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createAtom<T>(initialValue: T): Atom<T>
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `initialValue` | `T` | Yes | Initial typed value. |

## Returns

An `Atom<T>` with camelCase `get()`, `set()`, `update()`, `subscribe()`, `delete()`, and `isDeleted()` methods.

## Usage
```luau
local Level = Reactily.createAtom(0.7)
local Connection = Level.subscribe(function(change: Reactily.AtomChange<number>)
    print(change.previous, change.current)
end)
Level.set(0.9)
Connection.disconnect()
Level.delete()
```

## Understanding this API

An atom represents one writable value outside the component-local hook state. Other code can subscribe to changes.

### Practical guidance

Use it for small pieces of shared data. Keep a single atom instance for each logical value; recreating an atom loses its earlier subscriptions and state.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use an atom when a small value needs to be shared outside any one component.

### Behavior and ownership

Subscribers observe changes through the atom’s own API, independently of component-local `useState`.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Store the returned atom in a stable module or owner; recreating it discards subscriptions and the existing value.

`createFrame` creates a **virtual element**, not an immediate Roblox `Frame` Instance. A render root mounts and updates its underlying Roblox Instance.

## Signature

```luau
Reactily.createFrame(props: FrameProps?, children: {Element}?): Element
```

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `props` | `FrameProps?` | Frame properties such as `Size`, `Position`, and `BackgroundColor3`. |
| `children` | `{Element}?` | Optional virtual children rendered inside the frame. |

## Example

```luau
local Panel = Reactily.createFrame({
    Size = UDim2.fromOffset(360, 140),
    Position = UDim2.fromOffset(20, 20),
    BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(30, 35, 42),
    BorderSizePixel = 0,
}, {
    Reactily.createTextLabel({
        Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1),
        BackgroundTransparency = 1,
        Text = "Hello, Roblox",
    }),
})

Root.render(Panel)
```

This example assumes `Reactily` and `Root` were initialized as shown in [Getting Started](/docs/getting-started).

## Property naming

Roblox property names stay in PascalCase: `BackgroundColor3`, not `backgroundColor3`. Public Luau types are also PascalCase, such as `Reactily.FrameProps`.

## Related

[Rendering](/docs/concepts/rendering) · [createRoot](/docs/api/virtual-tree/create-root) · [Examples](/docs/guides/examples)

## Understanding this API

`createFrame` is the normal building block for grouping UI elements. It describes a Frame without creating it until the root renders.

### Practical guidance

Place child elements in the optional children array. Use official Roblox properties such as `Size`, `Position`, and `BackgroundColor3` inside the props table.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use `createFrame` for containers, grouping elements, and defining UI regions using Roblox Frame properties.

### Behavior and ownership

Properties are passed in a table and applied when Reactily mounts or reconciles the element.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Keep native Roblox prop keys PascalCase (`Size`, `Position`, `BackgroundColor3`). Reactily-specific metadata keys are defined by their typed props.

title: Reactily.createRoot
sidebar_label: createRoot
sidebar_position: 6
description: Mount and manage one Reactily UI tree under a Roblox Instance.
---

`createRoot` connects a virtual Reactily tree to a Roblox parent such as `PlayerGui`. Its root owns rendering and cleanup for that tree.

## Signature

```luau
Reactily.createRoot(parent: Instance): Root
```

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `parent` | `Instance` | Roblox Instance where the rendered tree belongs. |

## Example: mount a panel

```luau
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Reactily = require(ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Reactily"))

local PlayerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local Root = Reactily.createRoot(PlayerGui)

Root.render(Reactily.createFrame({
    Size = UDim2.fromOffset(300, 120),
    BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(30, 35, 42),
}))
```

Run the example in a client `LocalScript`. Rendering again on the same root updates the existing tree through reconciliation.

## Cleanup

```luau
Root.delete()
```

Call `delete()` when the interface is permanently dismissed. Do not call `render()` on a deleted root.

## Version 2.1.0 conventions

The root render method is lowercase **`Root.render()`**, not `Root.Render()`; cleanup is **`Root.Delete()`**, not `Root.delete()`. Reactily public functions such as `createRoot()` are camelCase; exported types and Roblox host properties are PascalCase.

## Related

[Getting Started](/docs/getting-started) · [Rendering](/docs/concepts/rendering) · [createFrame](/docs/api/typed-creators/create-frame)

## Understanding this API

A root manages the reconciliation lifecycle under a specific Roblox parent. `render` sets the virtual tree that the root should display.

### Practical guidance

Keep the root handle while the UI exists, and call its deletion method when the owner is destroyed. Updating the same root lets Reactily reconcile changes instead of creating a new root for every update.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Create one root for each Roblox parent that Reactily should manage. Render elements through that root instead of creating duplicate UI parents on each state change.

### Behavior and ownership

A root is an owner of rendered instances and associated component state. Hold on to it until the interface is no longer needed.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Creating a new root on every render can create duplicate UI and leave old roots active. Keep the root stable and dispose of it when its host is removed.

# `Reactily.createVirtualList`

Creates a small stateful virtual-list virtualRange controller.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.createVirtualList(itemCount: number, itemSize: number, viewportSize: number, overscan: number?): VirtualList
```
## Usage
```luau
local list = Reactily.createVirtualList(
	1000,
	36,
	400,
	2
)
```
## Works with

Pairs naturally with `resolveVirtualList`, `sliceVirtualList`, keyed elements.

## Understanding this API

This retains a small controller for virtual list calculations across scroll updates.

### Practical guidance

Keep the same controller while the list configuration remains relevant; pass updated offsets to calculate the visible range.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this creator when you need the VirtualList capability described above, and keep its result under a clear owner.

### Behavior and ownership

Virtualization limits the rendered content to the portion needed for the visible region.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Use stable item identity when mapping virtual entries to elements to avoid unnecessary remounts.

# `Reactily.resolveVirtualList`

Calculates the visible fixed-size list range plus overscan.

## Signature
```luau
Reactily.resolveVirtualList(
	itemCount: number,
	itemSize: number,
	scrollOffset: number,
	viewportSize: number,
	overscan: number?
): VirtualRange
```
## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | :---: | --- |
| `itemCount` | `number` | Yes | Total number of logical items in the virtualized list. |
| `itemSize` | `number` | Yes | Fixed pixel size of one virtual-list item. Must be greater than zero. |
| `scrollOffset` | `number` | Yes | Current scroll position in pixels. |
| `viewportSize` | `number` | Yes | Visible viewport size in pixels. |
| `overscan` | `number?` | No | Optional number of extra virtual-list rows rendered before and after the visible range. |

## Returns

A virtual-list range containing `first`, `last`, `offset`, and `totalSize`.

## Usage
```luau
local range = Reactily.resolveVirtualList(
	5000,
	44,
	scrollingFrame.CanvasPosition.Y,
	scrollingFrame.AbsoluteWindowSize.Y,
	3
)
```

## Understanding this API

Given scrolling measurements, this calculates the index range that intersects the viewport.

### Practical guidance

Use the resulting indices to mount visible rows and position them at the correct offsets inside the full scroll area.

## Additional usage notes

### When to use it

Use this helper when calculates the visible fixed-size list range plus overscan.

### Behavior and ownership

Virtualization limits the rendered content to the portion needed for the visible region.

### Pitfalls to avoid

> **Note:** Use stable item identity when mapping virtual entries to elements to avoid unnecessary remounts.

# Lifecycle

Reactily-owned resources use `delete()` and `isDeleted()`.
```luau
local Root = Reactily.createRoot(playerGui)

-- Later:
Root.delete()
```
Calling `Delete()` on an owned resource should:

1. disconnect owned connections,
2. stop owned runtime work,
3. release owned Instances/resources,
4. make repeated deletion safe.

Roblox-owned resources retain Roblox names:
```luau
instance:Destroy()
Connection:Disconnect()
```
## Ownership rule

The object that creates or adopts a resource should have an obvious cleanup path for that resource.

## Idle behavior

Reactily is designed so idle UI does not require a permanent self-generated frame loop. Continuous work should exist only while a feature such as an active animation genuinely needs it.

sidebar_position: 1
title: Rendering
description: Understand roots, virtual elements, components, and keyed updates.
---

Reactily renders Roblox UI by turning virtual element descriptions into Instances. Your components describe **what the UI should look like**, while the renderer creates and reconciles the actual Roblox objects.

## Roots and ownership

Start with a `PlayerGui`, `SurfaceGui`, or another appropriate Roblox parent. A [render root](/docs/api/virtual-tree/create-root) owns the Reactily tree mounted underneath it.

```luau
local Root = Reactily.createRoot(PlayerGui)
Root.render(Reactily.createFrame({
    Size = UDim2.fromOffset(320, 180),
}))
```

## Virtual elements and typed creators

Typed creators such as `createFrame`, `createTextLabel`, and `createTextButton` describe Roblox GUI objects. These calls do not immediately create Instances.

All Roblox host properties use **PascalCase**.

## Function components

A component is a Luau function that returns an element. Use components to group and reuse UI behavior.

```luau
type GreetingProps = {
    Name: string,
}

local function Greeting(props: GreetingProps): Reactily.Element
    return Reactily.createTextLabel({
        Size = UDim2.fromOffset(240, 44),
        Text = `Hello, {props.Name}`,
    })
end

Root.render(Reactily.createComponent(Greeting, { Name = "Lily" }))
```

Components can use hooks such as [useState](/docs/api/hooks/use-state) to update UI from local state.

## Reconciliation and keys

When you render a new virtual tree, Reactily compares it with the previous one instead of blindly remounting every object. For lists whose items move, insert, or disappear, provide stable keys so item identities survive reordering.

## Portals

A portal renders a subtree into a different Roblox parent while maintaining the logical relationship of the component tree. Use it for overlays or UI hosted outside the normal parent.

## Cleanup

Call `Root.Delete()` to release the root (`Root.render()` intentionally remains lowercase). For more detail see [Lifecycle](/docs/concepts/lifecycle) and [Examples](/docs/guides/examples).

# State & Reactivity

Reactily exposes component state and standalone reactive primitives.

## Hooks
```luau
local count, setCount = Reactily.useState(0)
```
Hooks must be called in a stable order for every render of a component.

## Atoms

Atoms are useful outside component-local state:
```luau
local count = Reactily.createAtom(0)

local Connection = count.subscribe(function(change: Reactily.AtomChange<number>)
    print(change.current)
end)

count.set(1)
Connection.disconnect()
count.delete()
```
Reactily avoids downstream work when the resolved value has not changed.

## Stores and selectors

Stores group related state. Selectors subscribe to a derived slice so unrelated updates do not force unnecessary work.

## Bindings and signals

Bindings represent reactive values that can feed UI props. Signals are event-style reactive primitives with explicit ownership and cleanup.

# Getting Started

## Install Reactily

Mount the Reactily package where your client code can require it. The supported package entry point is:
```text
src/init.luau
```
For this example, expose the package ModuleScript as `ReplicatedStorage.Reactily` and run the code from a `LocalScript`:
```luau
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Reactily = require(ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Reactily"))
local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local playerGui = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
```
## Create a root

A root owns one rendered Reactily tree.
```luau
local Root = Reactily.createRoot(playerGui)
```
## Create a component
```luau
type CounterProps = {
	InitialValue: number,
}

local function Counter(props: CounterProps): Reactily.Element
	local count, setCount = Reactily.useState(props.InitialValue)

	return Reactily.createTextButton({
		Size = UDim2.fromOffset(240, 64),
		Text = `Count: {count}`,

		OnActivated = function()
			setCount(function(previous: number): number
				return previous + 1
			end)
		end,
	})
end
```
## Render it
```luau
Root.render(
	Reactily.createComponent(Counter, {
		InitialValue = 0,
	})
)
```
## Update by rendering again
```luau
Root.render(nextElement)
```
Reactily reconciles the next tree with the current tree rather than rebuilding everything blindly.

## Clean up
```luau
Root.delete()
```
`Delete()` releases Reactily-owned work and rendered resources owned by the root.

The examples below use the Reactily v2.2.0 API. Public function names stay camelCase, exported types and Roblox host properties use PascalCase, and render roots expose `render()` and `delete()`.

## Before you begin

Install the published `Reactily.rbxm` package in `ReplicatedStorage`. Put the following setup in a `LocalScript` under `StarterPlayerScripts`:

```luau
--!strict
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local Reactily = require(ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("Reactily"))
local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local playerGui = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local root = Reactily.createRoot(playerGui)
```

Each rendering example can reuse this setup. Replace the previously rendered tree when trying a different example.

## Interactive counter

**Use this for:** Learning components, `useState`, and Roblox button events. The label changes when the player activates the button; no manual TextLabel updates are needed.

```luau
type CounterProps = {
    InitialValue: number,
}

local function Counter(props: CounterProps): Reactily.Element
    local count, setCount = Reactily.useState(props.InitialValue)

    return Reactily.createTextButton({
        Size = UDim2.fromOffset(240, 56),
        Text = `Count: {count}`,
        OnActivated = function()
            setCount(function(previous: number): number
                return previous + 1
            end)
        end,
    })
end

root.render(Reactily.createComponent(Counter, {
    InitialValue = 0,
}))
```

The state setter receives the previous value, avoiding a stale captured count when updates are queued. [Read the useState API](/docs/api/hooks/use-state).

## Frame with child content

**Use this for:** A simple panel with Roblox-native dimensions and colors. The frame and label are virtual elements until they are passed to a render root.

```luau
local Panel = Reactily.createFrame({
    Size = UDim2.fromOffset(340, 150),
    Position = UDim2.fromOffset(24, 24),
    BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(27, 34, 40),
    BorderSizePixel = 0,
}, {
    Reactily.createTextLabel({
        Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1),
        BackgroundTransparency = 1,
        Text = "Welcome to Reactily",
        TextColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(240, 247, 250),
    }),
})

root.render(Panel)
```

[Frame creator reference](/docs/api/typed-creators/create-frame) explains the arguments and return value.

## Standalone atom

**Use this for:** Shared reactive state outside a component. Atoms notify subscribers when their stored value changes.

```luau
local CounterAtom = Reactily.createAtom(0)
local Connection = CounterAtom.subscribe(function(change: Reactily.AtomChange<number>)
    print("Count:", change.current)
end)

CounterAtom.set(1)
Connection.disconnect()
```

Subscriptions must be cleaned up when no longer needed. Check the [atom reference](/docs/api/state/create-atom) for its precise subscription contract.

## Virtual list range

**Use this for:** Long inventories, search results, or menus where only visible rows should be mounted. Calculating a range does not automatically render or recycle rows.

```luau
local ItemCount = 5000
local RowHeight = 44
local ScrollOffset = 250
local ViewportHeight = 420
local Overscan = 3

local Range = Reactily.resolveVirtualList(
    ItemCount,
    RowHeight,
    ScrollOffset,
    ViewportHeight,
    Overscan
)

print(Range.first, Range.last, Range.totalSize)
```

Use the returned range to choose which items to create. [Virtual list reference](/docs/api/virtualization/resolve-virtual-list).

## Animation

**Use this for:** Changing properties of an actual Roblox Instance with an owned animation. Unlike virtual elements, the first argument must be a mounted Instance.

```luau
local Frame = Instance.new("Frame")
Frame.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(240, 120)
Frame.BackgroundTransparency = 1
Frame.Parent = playerGui

local Animation = Reactily.playTween(Frame, {
    BackgroundTransparency = 0,
}, {
    Time = 0.25,
    EasingStyle = Enum.EasingStyle.Quad,
    EasingDirection = Enum.EasingDirection.Out,
})

-- When this animation is no longer needed:
-- Animation.delete()
```

[Animation reference](/docs/api/animation/play-tween) covers the owned animation handle.

## Render root cleanup

**Use this for:** Closing an interface or disposing of a local UI controller.

```luau
root.delete()
```

Do not continue rendering into a root after deleting it. Use Roblox's own `:Destroy()` and `:Disconnect()` methods for Roblox-owned resources.

# Performance

Reactily's performance model is based on avoiding work rather than trying to make unnecessary work cheaper.

## Change-only updates

Do not write state, props, callbacks, or Instances again when the resolved value is unchanged.

## Keyed reconciliation

Stable keys let Reactily preserve child identity during list changes.

## Virtualization

Use virtual lists/grids when only a small window of a large collection is visible.

## Runtime work

Schedulers and animation systems should disconnect or become dormant when there is no pending work.

## Cleanup symmetry

Every subscription, scheduled callback, animation, pooled object, and root should have a matching cleanup path.

# React 19.3 parity

Reactily is React-inspired, not a DOM renderer. The current documentation site itself runs on React 19.3, while the Roblox runtime exposes the React-style concepts that make sense for Roblox Instances and Luau.

## Current Reactily equivalents

Reactily v2.1.0 (API v1) already includes modern state and concurrency-style APIs:

```luau
Reactily.useActionState
Reactily.useOptimistic
Reactily.useEffectEvent
Reactily.useDeferredValue
Reactily.useTransition
Reactily.startTransition
Reactily.Suspense
Reactily.lazy
Reactily.memo
Reactily.forwardRef
Reactily.createContext
```

It also includes Roblox-specific hooks that do not exist in React DOM:

```luau
Reactily.useCurrentCamera
Reactily.useDevice
Reactily.useLocalPlayer
Reactily.useMeasure
Reactily.useProperty
Reactily.useShortcut
Reactily.useTag
```

## APIs mapped to Roblox

Reactily v2.1.0 includes Roblox-native `ViewTransition` and Fragment ref capabilities. These do not render browser DOM snapshots; they operate on Reactily elements and Roblox Instances. For transition configuration, see the [`createViewTransition` API](/docs/api/animation/create-view-transition). The package also exposes the `FragmentInstance` type.

React DOM's `browser()` and Trusted Types support are also web/server-rendering features and do not map to Roblox clients.

## Compatibility rule

New React-inspired functionality should be additive throughout Reactily 2.x. Existing public names and behavior remain supported, deprecated APIs get a migration period, and intentionally breaking changes wait for the next major release.

# Introduction

## What is Reactily?

Reactily is a typed, React-inspired interface framework for Roblox Luau.

It provides virtual elements, function components, hooks, keyed reconciliation, reactive state, stores, signals, bindings, themes, animation systems, virtualization, object pools, diagnostics, and explicit lifecycle ownership through one public package.

Reactily is designed for developers who want component-driven UI without giving up direct control over Roblox Instances, cleanup, and runtime behavior.

## Why use it?

- **Strict typed API:** Public contracts are designed for `--!strict`, autocomplete, and clear ownership.
- **Component-driven UI:** Build interfaces from reusable function components and virtual elements.
- **Explicit lifecycle:** Reactily-owned resources use `.delete()` / `.isDeleted()` instead of hiding cleanup.
- **Change-only work:** State, UI, and runtime systems avoid work when the resolved value has not changed.
- **Idle-safe runtime:** Continuous work exists only while a feature actually needs it.
- **Roblox-aware:** Reactily keeps Roblox lifecycle and method conventions where Roblox owns the object.

## When should I not use it?

Reactily may not be the right fit when:

- the interface is tiny enough that direct Instance construction is simpler,
- your codebase does not need component composition or reactive state,
- your team prefers a fully imperative UI architecture,
- you do not want to adopt stable hook ordering and explicit Reactily ownership.

## How do I get started?

1. Read [Getting Started](./getting-started.md).
2. Learn the core concepts in [Rendering](./concepts/rendering.md), [State & Reactivity](./concepts/state.md), and [Lifecycle](./concepts/lifecycle.md).
3. Use the [API reference](/api) when you need an exact function signature or usage example.
4. Review [Examples](./guides/examples.md) for practical patterns.

## API conventions

Reactily public functions use camelCase dot calls; owned resource methods use the exact casing of their exported type:
```luau
local Root = Reactily.createRoot(playerGui)

Root.render(Element)
Root.delete()
```
Roblox-owned APIs keep Roblox syntax:
```luau
Connection:Disconnect()
instance:Destroy()
instance:SetAttribute("enabled", true)
```

# Documentation Authoring

Reactily's website reads the Markdown files in `reactily-website/src/content/`. Its API reference is **not** generated by Moonwave at runtime.

## Source of truth

The release's public exports are declared in `scripts/init.luau` and shipped in the `Reactily.rbxm` ModuleScript. Use that public API and its referenced Luau modules when documenting method names, return types, event callbacks, and ownership.

For Reactily v2.1.0, public top-level functions generally use camelCase (such as `Reactily.createRoot` and `Reactily.useState`). Module namespace methods and owned-handle methods use their exported PascalCase names (such as `Reactily.Layout.Grid`, `Root.Delete`, and `Animation.Play`). The root's `render` method is specifically lowercase: `Root.render`.

Roblox Instance properties such as `BackgroundColor3`, `Size`, `Position`, and supported event properties such as `OnActivated` retain PascalCase.

## Write an API page

Put an API page under the matching `src/content/api/` category. Keep its existing `title: Reactily.apiName` frontmatter aligned with the exact public export. Use real Luau syntax and verified signatures, not guessed internal type names.

````markdown
---
title: Reactily.createRoot
description: Mounts a Reactily tree under a Roblox Instance.
---

## Usage

```luau
local Root = Reactily.createRoot(PlayerGui)
Root.render(Element)
Root.delete()
```
````

Describe ownership and cleanup for returned handles. Update examples when their signatures change.

## Published versions

Published documentation is snapshotted from the **exact Git release tag**. Changing Markdown on `main` does not rewrite an existing release archive. To make newer documentation available under a new tag, include the Markdown changes in that release's commit before publishing it.

## Checks

Run `npm run validate:api` and `npm run validate:links` from `reactily-website` to catch missing public API pages and broken links. These checks do not replace verifying methods and examples against the shipped RBXM.
